Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 91, verses 1–8:

﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾. Al-Duha (الضحى) is the rising and full strength of light. Al-Duha' (الضحاء), with a fatha on the ḍād and a long vowel, is the period after that until the zawal (زوال, the sun's decline after its zenith). It is also said that al-Duha means the whole of the day, but the first meaning is the one known in the language. ﴿And the moon when it follows it﴾, that is, it comes after it. Regarding its following of the sun there are three opinions. The first: it follows it in the abundance of light, since it is the brightest of the heavenly bodies after the sun, especially on the night of the full moon. The second: it follows it in its rising, since it rises after the sun sets, and this is in the first half of the month. The third is that the subject of the verb (the pronoun) refers to the day, because the sun is made clear by the day, so it is as if the day is what displayed it. It is also said that the pronoun as subject refers to God, and it is said that the pronoun as object refers to the darkness, or the earth, or the world. All of this is far-fetched, because there is nothing preceding that the pronoun could refer back to. ﴿And the night when it covers it﴾, that is, it covers it. The pronoun as object refers to the sun, and the pronoun as subject refers to the night, according to the most correct view. ﴿And the sky and He who built it﴾. It is said that ما in His words "wa ma banahā" (and what built it), "wa ma ṭaḥāhā" (and what spread it out), and "wa ma sawwāhā" (and what fashioned it) are relative pronouns meaning "man" (من), and the intended meaning is God, the Exalted. It is also said that they are verbal-nominal (maṣdariyya), as if he said: "and the sky and its building." Al-Zamakhshari weakened this with his words: "fa-alhamahā" (then He inspired it), because the intended meaning there is unanimously God, and this view leads to a corruption of the composition. Some scholars also weakened the view that they are relative pronouns, by placing the mention of created things before the Creator. If it is asked: why did he turn away from "man" to the word "ma" in the view that considers them relative pronouns? The answer: he did this to intend the attributive sense, as if he said "and the Mighty One who built it." ﴿Spread it out﴾, that is, He extended it. ﴿And the soul and He who fashioned it﴾. The fashioning of the soul is the perfection of its intellect and understanding. If it is asked: why was "nafs" (soul) made indefinite? The answer has two aspects. The first: he intended the genus, as in His words: ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. The second: he intended the soul of Adam. The first is the preferred view. ﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾, that is, He made it aware of the path of wickedness and the path of piety, and He gave it a capacity by which it is possible to acquire either of the two matters. It is possible that the waw here has the meaning of "or," as in His words: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3].

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 91, verses 9–12:

﴿Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies it﴾ This is the response to the oath according to the majority (al-jumhur). Al-Zamakhshari said: the response is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "Allah will surely destroy the people of Makkah for their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as He destroyed the people of Thamud for their denial of Salih (peace be upon him)." He said: as for "qad aflaha" it is a statement that follows His words ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ by way of digression (istitrad). This is far-fetched. The subject of "zakkaha" is a pronoun referring back to "man," and the meaning is: "Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies himself," that is, cleanses it from sins and defects. It was said that the subject is a pronoun for Allah, the Exalted, but the first is more apparent. ﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾, meaning he belittles it with disbelief and disobedience. Its root is d-s-s, meaning "to conceal," as if he concealed himself when he belittled it. The final sin (s) was replaced by a weak letter (ʿillah), as in their saying "qassayt adhfari" (I trimmed my nails), whose original form is "qasasttu." ﴿With its transgression﴾: it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of tughyan (transgression); the yaʾ in it was changed to a waw in accordance with the dialect of those who say "tughayt." The preposition bi- is either like your saying "I wrote with the pen," or causal, and the meaning is "because of its transgression." Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is Thamud by their punishment, and his words support it: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5]. ﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: the governing element of "idh" is either "kadhdhabat" or "tughwaha." The meaning of "unbaʿatha" is that he went out to hamstring the she-camel swiftly and eagerly. "Ashqaha" refers to the one who hamstrung the she-camel, the red-faced one of Thamud, whose name was Qudar ibn Salif. It is possible that "ashqaha" refers to a group, since the comparative form (afʿal), when made genitive by an attached noun, is the same for singular and plural; but the first (singular) reading is more apparent and more well-known.

The subject of "zakkaha" is a pronoun referring back to "man," and the meaning is: "Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies himself," that is, cleanses it from sins and defects. It was said that the subject is a pronoun for Allah, the Exalted, but the first is more apparent. ﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾, meaning he belittles it with disbelief and disobedience. Its root is d-s-s, meaning "to conceal," as if he concealed himself when he belittled it. The final sin (s) was replaced by a weak letter (ʿillah), as in their saying "qassayt adhfari" (I trimmed my nails), whose original form is "qasasttu." ﴿With its transgression﴾: it is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of tughyan (transgression); the yaʾ in it was changed to a waw in accordance with the dialect of those who say "tughayt." The preposition bi- is either like your saying "I wrote with the pen," or causal, and the meaning is "because of its transgression." Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is Thamud by their punishment, and his words support it: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5]. ﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: the governing element of "idh" is either "kadhdhabat" or "tughwaha." The meaning of "unbaʿatha" is that he went out to hamstring the she-camel swiftly and eagerly. "Ashqaha" refers to the one who hamstrung the she-camel, the red-faced one of Thamud, whose name was Qudar ibn Salif. It is possible that "ashqaha" refers to a group, since the comparative form (afʿal), when made genitive by an attached noun, is the same for singular and plural; but the first (singular) reading is more apparent and more well-known.

﴿Then the Messenger of God said to them﴾, meaning Salih (peace be upon him). ﴿The she-camel of God and her drink﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose estimated form is "احفظوا ناقة الله" (guard the she-camel of God), or "احذروا ناقة الله وسقياها" (beware the she-camel of God and her drink), meaning her share of the water.

﴿So they hamstrung her﴾: the hamstringing is attributed to the group because they agreed upon it, although only one of them carried it out.

﴿So He destroyed them completely﴾: this is an expression for sending down punishment upon them, and it carries an element of awe.

﴿And He leveled them﴾, that is, because of their sin, which is denial or the hamstringing of the she-camel.

On ﴿And He leveled them﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is that He leveled the tribe in destruction, so that none of them escaped. al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun refers to the destruction, meaning He leveled it among them.

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: the pronoun of the subject refers to God, Exalted, and the pronoun in "عقباها" (its consequence) refers to the destruction and the leveling, which is annihilation. The meaning is that He does not fear the outcome of their destruction, and no one can call Him to account for it, unlike kings who fear the consequences of their actions. In this there is a belittling of them. It has also been said that the pronoun of the subject refers to Salih, but this is far-fetched.

It was recited ﴿so he does not fear﴾ with the fa' (فلا يخاف) and also with the waw (ولا يخاف). It has been said that in the recitation with the waw, the subject is "أشقاها" (the most wretched of them). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: he set out and did not fear the consequence of his deed. This is far-fetched.
